oidc_jwt.description: Dex can intentionally issue an ID token whose aud claim is a different client than the one that initiated login when the target client explicitly trusts the requesting client via trustedPeers and the dynamic audience scope is requested.
oidc_jwt.source: custom-scopes-claims-clients.md Cross-client trust and authorized party
oidc_jwt.note: Do not flag cross-client audience changes as overbroad authorization when trustedPeers is configured; this is a documented feature.

oidc_jwt.description: Dex does not issue refresh tokens for SAML connector logins and ignores offline_access for SAML.
oidc_jwt.note: Absence of refresh_token after SAML-backed login is by design, not a token issuance bug.

oidc_jwt.description: Dex rotates refresh tokens on every refresh by default and may optionally allow limited reuse via reuseInterval or disable rotation explicitly.
oidc_jwt.source: configuration/tokens.md Refresh tokens and Expiration and rotation settings
oidc_jwt.note: A changed refresh token value after refresh is expected behavior, not session confusion.

oidc_jwt.description: Authorization code flow requests without a nonce may succeed.
oidc_jwt.note: Do not flag missing nonce acceptance in pure code flow as a vulnerability by itself.

oidc_jwt.description: Each refresh of an ID token issues a new refresh token by design.
oidc_jwt.note: Reuse of an old refresh token after a successful refresh may fail by design.

oidc_jwt.description: The authproxy connector consumes configured proxy headers such as X-Remote-User and X-Remote-Group and relies on the front-end proxy to strip client-supplied headers.
oidc_jwt.note: Header-based identity injection is only a vulnerability if the deployment fails to strip untrusted headers; the connector behavior itself is documented.

oidc_jwt.description: Admin changes to upstream OIDC connector issuer, discovery overrides, or client configuration are expected to affect subsequent authentications.
oidc_jwt.note: Do not flag successful authentication under newly configured trust anchors as a coherence bug; only continued acceptance of old trust after change is suspicious.

oidc_jwt.description: Password grant is optional and will not work unless explicitly enabled with grantTypes including password and passwordConnector configured.
oidc_jwt.note: Password grant failures on instances without this configuration are expected.

oidc_jwt.description: Dex trust anchors, clients, connectors, and OAuth behavior are configured administratively via config/gRPC, and new logins under updated configuration are expected to follow the new settings.
oidc_jwt.note: Do not flag a login that succeeds or fails under newly applied admin configuration as a coherence bug; only acceptance of old trust after explicit rotation is suspicious.

oidc_jwt.description: OIDC connector group claims only refresh when the ID token is refreshed; regular refresh flow does not update groups claims.
oidc_jwt.note: Group changes not appearing immediately in refreshed tokens can be by design and should not be misread as stale authorization cache unless the test specifically forces re-evaluation.

oidc_jwt.description: Changing OIDC connector settings such as issuer, issuerAlias, discovery overrides, or getUserInfo changes subsequent login behavior by design.
oidc_jwt.note: A login succeeding or failing after an admin reconfiguration is expected; only acceptance of old trust after explicit rotation/rebinding should be treated as suspicious.

oidc_jwt.constraint: Dex does not expose documented REST admin endpoints for enabling auth methods, configuring JWT validation, creating roles, policies, groups, applications, or users. These are configured statically in Dex config files or via the gRPC API, not via HTTP JSON admin APIs. Do NOT invent REST setup calls for oidc_jwt testing on Dex.

Token exchange is supported only with the OIDC connector. For oidc_jwt token_exchange tests, the upstream connector MUST be type=oidc and the oauth2.grantTypes configuration MUST include urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange (enabled by default if grantTypes is omitted).

For token_exchange using upstream access tokens, the OIDC connector MUST set getUserInfo=true if the upstream access token is opaque or lacks needed claims. Without getUserInfo, Dex may be unable to validate or enrich the subject token correctly.
Dex token exchange requires connector_id in the form body in addition to the RFC 8693 parameters. Omitting connector_id makes the request invalid for Dex-specific upstream selection.

Dex binds issued tokens to OAuth clients. For token exchange, the client id/secret pair must be supplied via HTTP Basic Authentication to /token even when the client is marked public in Dex configuration. Do NOT assume anonymous token exchange.

Password grant works only when oauth2.passwordConnector is configured and grantTypes includes password. A failed password-grant login without passwordConnector configured is a setup error, not a security rejection.

Dex supports refresh token rotation by default: every refresh of an ID token issues a new refresh token. If testing replay or reuse behavior of refresh tokens, account for rotation semantics. reuseInterval allows reuse of the previous refresh token only within the configured interval; disableRotation disables per-request rotation and should be treated as an explicit security tradeoff, not a bug.

Numeric sentinel analysis: oauth2.grantTypes omitted means Dex enables default grant types authorization_code, refresh_token, and urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange. Do NOT treat omission as 'deny all grants'; omission selects a non-empty default.

Numeric sentinel analysis: Google connector promptType set to empty string "" disables Dex's default prompt=consent behavior and falls back to Google's default behavior. Do NOT assume empty string means literal empty prompt semantics identical to omission.

For I1 trust_anchor_substitution and issuer-validation tests against Dex as an RP consuming upstream OIDC tokens, configure the OIDC connector issuer field explicitly and ensure the upstream token's iss matches that configured issuer. Dex documentation states issuer MUST match provider discovery; issuerAlias exists only for off-spec providers. A mismatch rejection is expected; acceptance without proper issuer binding would be the bug.

For I1 oidc_sso_audience_cross_tenant tests, use two distinct OIDC connector configurations with different clientIDs. The upstream id_token aud MUST match the connector's configured clientID per OIDC validation expectations. Reusing the same clientID across connectors invalidates the test oracle.

For I2 expired_token and future_token tests on upstream OIDC token exchange, include a CONTROL exchange using a valid upstream token alongside the attack token. Without a control, a failed exchange may reflect broken connector configuration, missing getUserInfo, or wrong client auth rather than correct time validation.

For I2 replay_same_token on plain JWT/OIDC bearer tokens, do NOT flag successful reuse of the same upstream token as a vulnerability by itself. Dex documentation describes stateless token exchange and OIDC flows; JWT jti tracking is not documented as enforced. Treat replay of ordinary bearer JWTs as by-design unless the tested context is a one-time artifact such as an authorization code.

For I3 state_swap and flow-coherence tests, the authorization request state value must be session-bound by the client application, not Dex alone. Dex returns state to the client callback, but the relying client must verify it. A failure in the client-side state check is outside Dex's broker API unless the same Dex-issued code can be redeemed across mismatched sessions.

For I3 code replay tests, use the authorization_code flow and attempt to redeem the same code twice at /token. Dex certification results show codereuse tests as passed/warning-oriented; the correct oracle is HTTP failure on second redemption, not identity comparison.

For I3 config-change sequences involving grantTypes, connector settings, issuer changes, or client trust changes, admin configuration changes taking effect for NEW logins are by design. Only flag a violation if Dex continues accepting the OLD trust anchor or OLD code/token semantics after the configuration was explicitly changed.

For I5 token_exchange_scope_escalation tests, request only scopes that Dex documents as supported: openid, email, profile, groups, federated:id, offline_access, and audience:server:client_id:(client-id). Claims absent because the scope was never requested are not evidence of secure filtering; claims present beyond requested scope are the relevant signal.

For I5 cross-client audience tests, Dex supports cross-client trust via the dynamic scope audience:server:client_id:(client-id) only when the target client explicitly lists the requesting client in trustedPeers. Acceptance of cross-client audience without trustedPeers would be a bug; acceptance with trustedPeers is by design.

For I5 token_exchange_wrong_audience and token_exchange_ignore_audience tests, remember that Dex's token exchange request parameter audience is not documented as a standard enforced selector in the provided docs, while downstream token audience is primarily client-bound. The test must verify whether the resulting Dex-issued token is bound to the authenticated client/trusted peer relationship, not merely whether an arbitrary audience form field was accepted.

For OIDC request object tests, Dex certification notes unsigned request objects may be either correctly supported or rejected as unsupported. Do NOT treat rejection of request objects as a vulnerability. The vulnerability condition is acceptance of an unsigned request object with attacker-controlled authorization parameters when request objects are supported.

Dex documentation exposes dynamic management through gRPC API, not documented REST endpoints, for creating clients/users/connectors. Do NOT invent REST admin operations such as enable_auth_method, configure_jwt_validation, create_application, create_user, or modify_role_config from this documentation set; only the documented OIDC/OAuth2 runtime endpoints are available over HTTP.

For password-grant testing, /token with grant_type=password works ONLY when oauth2.grantTypes includes "password" and oauth2.passwordConnector is configured (for local users, typically passwordConnector=local). Without both, LOGIN_FAILED is expected and does not indicate a security issue.

For token_exchange testing, /token with grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange works only when oauth2.grantTypes includes the token-exchange grant. Dex enables it by default if grantTypes is omitted, but if grantTypes is explicitly set and omits token-exchange, exchange failures are expected.

Dex token exchange currently supports only the OIDC connector as upstream. For oidc_jwt tests, configure an OIDC connector and supply connector_id in the token exchange request. Testing token exchange against non-OIDC connectors will fail by design.

When exchanging upstream ACCESS tokens through Dex token exchange, the OIDC connector must have getUserInfo=true if identity claims are needed from access tokens. Access tokens are otherwise treated as opaque and may not be verifiable for exchange.
Dex requires connector_id on token exchange requests to select the upstream OIDC connector. Omitting connector_id can cause setup failure or ambiguous behavior unrelated to the invariant under test.
Dex /token requests use application/x-www-form-urlencoded bodies. The executor MUST send exchange_code_for_token, login_with_password, and token_exchange as form-encoded requests, not JSON.

Dex client authentication for /token is documented via HTTP Basic Authentication using client_id:client_secret, including token exchange and password grant examples. The fuzzer MUST provide valid client credentials as Basic auth for confidential clients; missing client auth can cause false failures unrelated to JWT validation.

Public clients in Dex may omit a secret, but redirect URI handling is restricted: if no redirectURIs are specified, public clients only support redirects beginning with http://localhost or urn:ietf:wg:oauth:2.0:oob. OIDC code-flow tests must use an allowed redirect URI for public clients.

For I2 expired_token and future_token tests against Dex as an OIDC RP via token exchange, include a CONTROL exchange using a valid upstream token from the same connector. Without a control, rejection of the attack token cannot be distinguished from broken connector/client configuration.

For I1/I5 cross-provider audience tests, create separate Dex OIDC connectors with distinct upstream client_ids and ensure the upstream token's aud is bound to the intended connector's client_id. A token minted for connector A presented with connector_id for connector B should be rejected; if the connectors share the same upstream client_id, the test is invalid.

Dex OIDC connector issuer must match the upstream provider discovery issuer exactly unless issuerAlias is explicitly configured for off-spec providers. For I1 issuer-validation tests, do not treat issuerAlias as a bypass bug; it is an explicit admin override.

Dex OIDC connector allowedGroups is exact list-membership filtering, not wildcard matching. For I4 multi-identity scenarios where multiple different users must authenticate through the same connector, OMIT allowedGroups unless all test identities are members of at least one identical allowed group. Do NOT set '*' expecting wildcard behavior.

Dex OIDC connector userIDKey and userNameKey select exact claim names, not patterns or matching rules. For I4 tests, these fields determine which upstream claim becomes the Dex identity. Changing them changes identity mapping by design; do not interpret that as identity confusion.

Dex OIDC connector claimMapping maps non-standard upstream claim names to standard claims by exact field name. It is not a wildcard or regex matcher. For I4/I5 tests, do not use '*' or pattern strings in claimMapping values; they will be treated as literal claim names.

Dex claimModifications.filterGroupClaims uses RE2 regex semantics, while allowedGroups uses exact membership checks. For I5 group-policy tests, distinguish regex-based group rewriting/filtering from exact allowlisting; otherwise false positives may occur when groups are transformed before issuance.

Dex claimModifications.newGroupFromClaims currently supports only string claims; non-string claims are skipped. For I5 numeric coercion tests, do not expect numeric upstream claims to participate in derived group creation.

Dex OIDC connector groups claims may be stale across refresh because groups only refresh when the ID token is refreshed, and insecureEnableGroups is disabled by default. For I3/I5 tests involving upstream group changes, use a fresh authentication/token exchange path that re-evaluates upstream claims rather than assuming ordinary refresh updates groups.

Dex OIDC connector getUserInfo causes UserInfo claims to take priority over ID Token claims. For I4/I5 tests, keep this setting fixed within a sequence; otherwise identity/claim differences after reconfiguration are by-design config changes, not flow incoherence.

Dex supports cross-client trust via the dynamic scope audience:server:client_id:(client-id), and the target client must explicitly list the requesting client in trustedPeers. For I5 audience/scope tests, a changed aud with matching azp can be by design when trustedPeers is configured.

Dex refresh token behavior includes rotation by default: every refresh issues a new refresh token. Tests that reuse an old refresh token without accounting for rotation may fail by design. If disableRotation or reuseInterval are configured, treat them as explicit admin choices, not replay vulnerabilities.

Numeric sentinel analysis: Dex duration settings are documented as explicit duration strings (e.g. 10m, 6h). The provided documentation does NOT define 0, "0s", or -1 as disable/default sentinels for expiry or leeway fields. The fuzzer MUST NOT assume zero or negative sentinel semantics for Dex token timing settings without instance-specific confirmation.
Dex does not document a token introspection or revocation HTTP endpoint in the provided docs. Do NOT treat absence of introspection/revocation as a security failure for oidc_jwt tests.

OIDC request-object testing: Dex certification notes show unsigned request objects may be either supported correctly or rejected as unsupported. For alg=none request-object tests, the oracle must accept either explicit rejection or correct secure handling; do NOT require support for request objects as a prerequisite.

OIDC code-flow nonce handling: Dex certification notes indicate code flow without nonce can succeed. Do NOT flag missing nonce on pure authorization-code requests as a vulnerability by itself; nonce is strongly relevant to ID token replay defenses, but Dex may not require it for code flow initiation.

Dex documentation states the product is configured exclusively from a config file and its dynamic management API is gRPC, not REST. For oidc_jwt testing, the fuzzer MUST NOT assume documented REST admin endpoints exist for enable_auth_method, configure_jwt_validation, create_auth_role, create_policy, revoke_session, cleanup_auth_method, or client/provider CRUD. Only the documented OIDC/OAuth HTTP endpoints (/auth, /token, /userinfo, discovery, keys) are available over HTTP.

For I2 expired_token and future_token tests against Dex as an OIDC provider, the fuzzer MUST include a control flow using a valid authorization request and successful code exchange. A failed attack flow alone is ambiguous because Dex may fail due to client misconfiguration, missing connector selection, or redirect URI mismatch rather than token freshness enforcement.

Dex's authorization endpoint supports standard OIDC request parameters including state and nonce. For I3 flow-coherence tests, the fuzzer MUST bind each authorization request to a unique state and verify the same state returns on callback. Dex documentation explicitly describes state as the defense linking the user who started the flow to the one who finished it and preventing replay.

Nonce is not universally required by Dex for code flow. Dex certification results explicitly include 'oidcc-ensure-request-without-nonce-succeeds-for-code-flow' as PASSED. Therefore, the fuzzer MUST NOT treat acceptance of a code-flow authorization request without nonce as a vulnerability by itself.

For OIDC request-object testing (I1 alg_none), Dex certification results indicate 'unsigned request object supported correctly or rejected as unsupported' is an open/unknown area. The fuzzer MUST treat two outcomes as acceptable by design: explicit rejection of unsigned request objects, or unsupported-request behavior. Only acceptance of an unsigned request object with attacker-controlled authorization parameters as a normal successful request should be considered suspicious.

For token exchange tests, Dex requires connector_id in addition to RFC 8693 parameters. The fuzzer MUST include connector_id naming the configured upstream OIDC connector; omitting it causes setup failure unrelated to security invariants.

Token exchange in Dex currently works only with the OIDC connector. The fuzzer MUST configure and target an OIDC upstream connector for oidc_jwt token-exchange tests; attempting token exchange through non-OIDC connectors is invalid setup, not a security failure.

When exchanging upstream access tokens rather than ID tokens, Dex requires getUserInfo=true on the upstream OIDC connector to validate/access claims from the access token. For token-exchange tests using subject_token_type=access_token, the fuzzer MUST enable getUserInfo or failures will be false positives caused by missing connector capability.

Dex token exchange requires client authentication via Basic Authentication even when the client is marked public for this use case. The fuzzer MUST send client_id/client_secret as HTTP Basic credentials when calling /token for token exchange; otherwise failures are setup errors.

Dex-issued tokens are client-bound. For I5 audience and cross-client tests, the fuzzer MUST vary the downstream client_id and requested scopes deliberately and interpret aud/azp according to Dex's cross-client trust model. A client may request an ID token for another client only when the target client explicitly lists the requester in trustedPeers.

For I5 cross-client audience tests, the fuzzer MUST distinguish normal cross-client trust from audience confusion. If scope includes audience:server:client_id:(target-client), Dex may legitimately issue an ID token with aud=target-client and azp=requesting-client, but only when the target client explicitly trusts the requester via trustedPeers.

Dex supports refresh token rotation by default: every refresh issues a new refresh token. The fuzzer MUST update stored refresh_token after each successful refresh. Reuse of an older refresh token may fail by design and is not itself evidence of replay protection bypass or breakage.

Numeric sentinel analysis for refresh token rotation settings: refreshTokens.disableRotation is a boolean switch, not a numeric sentinel; refreshTokens.reuseInterval is a duration and no special 0/-1 sentinel semantics are documented in the provided docs. The fuzzer MUST NOT assume 0 or -1 disables or tightens validation unless explicitly configured and documented elsewhere.

Dex documentation states some connectors do not support offline_access / refresh tokens, notably SAML and authproxy, and OAuth connector has no refresh support. For oidc_jwt tests that rely on refresh tokens, the fuzzer MUST use an upstream connector that supports refresh tokens, such as OIDC, and MUST NOT flag missing refresh_token on unsupported connectors as a vulnerability.

For upstream OIDC connector validation (Dex acting as RP), the configured issuer MUST match the issuer returned by upstream discovery unless issuerAlias is intentionally used for off-spec providers. For I1 issuer-validation tests, the fuzzer MUST know that issuerAlias is an explicit override; acceptance under a configured issuerAlias is by design, not an issuer-validation bypass.

For I1/I5 upstream audience-validation tests in token exchange or OIDC login, the fuzzer MUST configure distinct upstream clientIDs per connector when testing cross-provider or cross-tenant audience confusion. Dex documentation says the upstream OIDC connector uses clientID/clientSecret and issuer discovery; without distinct clientIDs, an audience-mismatch oracle is invalid.

For I5 scope-escalation tests, the fuzzer MUST request only Dex-supported scopes: openid, email, profile, groups, federated:id, offline_access, and audience:server:client_id:(client-id). Claims absent because the scope was never requested are not authorization failures, and claims present only because the scope was requested are not escalations.

Dex's UserInfo endpoint returns claims based on the authenticated session token. The fuzzer MUST use access_token as session_token for subsequent API calls. id_token is not the bearer credential for /userinfo.

For I4 identity-binding tests against Dex as OP, the stable principal is sub. Claims like email, preferred_username, and name may be mapped or transformed by upstream connector configuration (userIDKey, userNameKey, claimMapping, overrideClaimMapping, emailToLowercase, group modifications). The fuzzer MUST compare granted identity primarily using sub and treat other claims as potentially derived metadata.

Parameter matching semantics: allowedGroups on the upstream OIDC connector is documented as list-membership exact matching only. There is no companion type parameter for glob or regex. For multi-identity I4 scenarios where multiple different group values must pass the same connector, the fuzzer MUST OMIT allowedGroups rather than setting wildcard values like '*', which would be treated as a literal group name.

Parameter matching semantics: OIDC connector issuer is exact string match against discovery issuer unless issuerAlias is explicitly configured. There is no wildcard or regex mode. For I1 issuer tests, the fuzzer MUST use exact issuer values and MUST NOT assume partial or wildcard matching.

Parameter matching semantics: Microsoft connector tenant is exact match to one of common, consumers, organizations, or a specific tenant UUID/name. There is no wildcard mode. For multi-identity tests spanning tenants, the fuzzer MUST omit tenant restriction or create separate connectors; setting tenant='*' would not broaden matching.

Parameter matching semantics: group whitelists across Dex connectors (e.g., OIDC allowedGroups, Microsoft groups, GitLab groups, Bitbucket teams, Crowd groups) are exact list-membership constraints unless documentation explicitly says otherwise. For I4 multi-user tests, the fuzzer MUST NOT use wildcard strings to simulate 'any group'; omit the whitelist entirely instead.

Claim value type analysis: the provided Dex docs do not document generic bound-claim constraint parameters for JWT claim values on the downstream OP side. Therefore, the fuzzer SHOULD focus I5 numeric coercion tests on upstream claim transport and token exchange behavior rather than inventing unsupported bound_claims-style setup knobs.
